ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Counterfactual cue swaps to measure invented emotion evidence
PROPOSAL: Build a probing set from MAFW clips in which trained annotators list every audible and visible cue. For each clip, create counterfactual versions by muting the audio, masking the face region, or replacing the soundtrack with speech carrying a different emotion. Ask three open audiovisual language models to name the emotion and list supporting cues, then parse the cue lists with a fixed keyword lexicon so that scoring needs no external judge. Count cues listed by the model that the annotators did not mark as present, and count emotion changes when only an irrelevant cue changes.
CONTROLS: Compare against a text-only run on the same prompts, against a majority-label classifier, and against the unedited clips. Repeat decoding with five seeds and report the spread across seeds. Use a second annotator on two hundred clips to check the cue lists.
COST: 85
PREDICTION: Models should list absent cues far more often than the annotators do, and emotion answers should shift when an irrelevant cue is edited. The study fails to show the effect if text-only prompts already match the full-input rate of invented cues, or if annotators disagree on the cue lists.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Contrastive decoding against modality-dropped inputs
PROPOSAL: Reduce text-prior hallucination at inference time by contrasting the next-token distribution of the full audiovisual input with the distribution obtained when the clip is replaced by a blank frame and silence. Tokens that stay likely without the clip are penalised, so the explanation keeps only cues that the audio or the frames actually support. Apply the decoding rule to an open audiovisual language model on the DFEW and MAFW test clips, tune the penalty strength on a small validation split, and score the outputs with a keyword lexicon of annotated cues and with emotion keyword accuracy. No training is needed, so the method can be tried on any model whose logits are accessible.
CONTROLS: The comparison runs are greedy decoding, nucleus sampling, and the same contrastive rule with only the audio track dropped or only the frames dropped, all on the same clips and seeds. A shuffled-clip run, where the contrast input comes from a different clip, shows whether the gain comes from removing text priors or from plain regularisation of the distribution.
COST: 190
PREDICTION: Invented cues should fall while emotion keyword accuracy stays within a point of greedy decoding. The idea fails if the shuffled-clip contrast removes as many invented cues as the blank contrast, or if accuracy drops sharply.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cue-verified instruction data for emotion description models
PROPOSAL: Curate an instruction-tuning corpus whose captions have been verified against the clip. Start from MER and DFEW clips, let a pretrained audiovisual model draft emotion descriptions, then extract each cue the draft mentions and check it with a specialised detector: a speech-emotion classifier for prosody, a facial action unit detector for expressions, and an audio event tagger for ambient sound. Discard sentences whose cues no detector confirms, and keep the rest for fine-tuning a seven-billion-parameter model with low-rank adapters. Compare the behaviour of the tuned model on a held-out cue benchmark, analysing how often it mentions colour of clothing or background noise as evidence for an emotion, and recording the modelling choices that were tried.
CONTROLS: Controls are the same model tuned on unfiltered drafts, a model tuned on the same number of randomly dropped sentences, and the untuned model. Fix the learning rate, the number of updates and the clip set across runs, and repeat each run with three seeds.
COST: 420
PREDICTION: Filtered data should lower the share of unsupported cues relative to unfiltered drafts of equal size, without lowering emotion keyword recall. The result is refuted if randomly dropped sentences reduce unsupported cues by the same amount, or if the detectors themselves disagree with annotators too often.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reinforcement learning with a cue-grounding reward for emotion explanations
PROPOSAL: Fine-tune a multimodal large language model (MLLM) with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), rewarding explanations whose cited cues are confirmed by a verifier built from per-modality detectors. For each training clip the policy samples several explanations. The reward adds emotion keyword correctness to the fraction of cited cues that the facial action unit detector, the speech emotion recognition (SER) model and the audio event tagger support, and subtracts a penalty for each cue that none of them confirms. Training uses low-rank adaptation (LoRA) on the language backbone. Evaluate on a held-out clip set with human-annotated cues, reporting unsupported-cue rate and keyword accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare against the same model trained only on keyword correctness, against supervised fine-tuning on reference explanations, and against a reward that counts cited cues without verifying them. Hold the clips and the update count fixed, and run three seeds per setting.
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: The verified reward should cut unsupported cues while keeping keyword accuracy near the keyword-only run. It fails if the model learns to cite fewer cues overall without becoming more accurate about the ones it keeps.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Locating attention heads that import text priors in emotion explanations
PROPOSAL: Analyse an open seven-billion-parameter audiovisual model on DFEW clips for the heads whose attention to audio and frame tokens is weak while they write cue words. For each generated cue phrase, record the share of attention mass on the clip tokens per head, then select the heads with the lowest share and intervene by scaling their outputs down or boosting the heads with the highest clip share. Measure whether invented cues decrease and whether irrelevant but present cues, such as clothing colour or room noise, are cited less often as the reason for an emotion. Cue presence is checked against annotator lists, so no external judge is used.
CONTROLS: Compare the targeted intervention with scaling the same number of randomly chosen heads, and with no intervention. Repeat the head selection on two disjoint halves of the clips to test stability, and track keyword accuracy to see whether general quality is damaged.
COST: 130
PREDICTION: Boosting clip-attending heads should reduce invented cues more than scaling random heads. The idea fails if head selection does not transfer across the two halves, or if keyword accuracy falls as much as invented cues do.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training a cue verifier to filter emotion explanations
PROPOSAL: Train a lightweight verifier that reads a clip embedding and one cue statement and predicts whether the cue is present. Positive statements come from annotator cue lists on MAFW and DFEW, negatives from absent cues that commonly co-occur with the labelled emotion, such as tears with crying sounds. Use the verifier for rejection sampling: draw sixteen explanations per clip from an audiovisual language model, keep those whose cues all pass, and fine-tune on the kept ones. Evaluate unsupported-cue rate and emotion keyword accuracy on held-out clips, and report the verifier's own precision on absent but typical cues.
CONTROLS: Compare against fine-tuning on randomly kept explanations, against a verifier that sees only the text statement, and against the untuned model. Fix the sampling budget and the update count across runs, and use three seeds.
COST: 350
PREDICTION: A verifier that sees the clip should beat a text-only verifier on absent but typical cues by a clear gap in precision. The approach fails if the text-only verifier performs equally well, because then the filter would only copy language priors.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Conflict stimuli for testing which cue drives an emotion explanation
PROPOSAL: We construct conflict clips by pairing emotional speech from CREMA-D with face videos of a different emotion, and by adding irrelevant cues such as a bright jacket or street noise. We ask open audiovisual language models to name the emotion and justify it. Because we know which modality carries the labelled emotion in each clip, we can score automatically whether the justification cites the cue that actually explains the label, an irrelevant cue, or a cue absent from the input. We parse justifications with a fixed lexicon, so the evaluation needs no external language model and anyone can replay it. We then fine-tune one model on conflict clips with correct justifications and test it on unseen speakers.
CONTROLS: We compare the models against a text-only prompt and against clips where both modalities agree. We repeat every measurement with five seeds and check the lexicon parser against manual labels on two hundred justifications.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: We expect most justifications to cite the dominant modality of the model rather than the modality that carries the label. We would see the idea fail if the parser disagrees with manual labels or if agreeing clips show the same error rate as conflict clips.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Judge-free likelihood scoring of true and invented cue statements
PROPOSAL: Score audiovisual language models by the log-likelihood they assign to short statements about a clip, with no external judge. For every clip in DFEW and MAFW, write a true cue statement from annotator lists, an irrelevant but present cue statement, and an absent but typical statement such as tears accompanied by crying sounds. Compute length-normalised log-likelihood under each model with the clip and without it. A model that prefers absent typical statements over true ones with the clip present is relying on text priors. Release the statements and the scoring script so that evaluation is reproducible and cheap enough to run on every checkpoint during training.
CONTROLS: Compare the with-clip scores against the without-clip scores on the same statements, and against a language model of the same size that never sees the clip. Control for statement length and word frequency by matching pairs, and repeat across five paraphrases of each statement.
COST: 25
PREDICTION: Absent typical statements should receive clearly higher likelihood than irrelevant ones when the clip is removed, and the gap should shrink with the clip present. The metric is unusable if matched paraphrases change the ranking of models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Distractor augmentation to teach invariance to irrelevant cues
PROPOSAL: Teach a model to ignore irrelevant cues by editing training clips. Recolour clothing in frames, mix ambient street or cafe noise into the audio, and swap backgrounds, while leaving facial expression and voice prosody untouched. The target explanation stays the same for every edited version of a clip, so the only way to lower the loss is to rely on the cues that carry the emotion. Fine-tune an open audiovisual language model on MAFW and DFEW clips with low-rank adapters, then test on a benchmark in which the same irrelevant edits are applied at test time and in which new kinds of distractor are added. Report how often the stated emotion or the cited reason changes under edits.
CONTROLS: Compare against fine-tuning on unedited clips, against edits applied to the text instead of the clips, and against the untuned model. Hold the clip set and update count fixed, and repeat with three seeds.
COST: 270
PREDICTION: Edited-clip training should reduce answer changes under test-time edits and generalise partly to unseen distractor types. It fails if gains appear only for the exact edits used in training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hallucination rate versus amount of verified emotion data
PROPOSAL: Measure how unsupported cues and wrong reasons decline as the quantity of cue-verified instruction data grows. Build a verified corpus from MAFW and DFEW clips with detector-confirmed captions, then fine-tune an open audiovisual model with low-rank adapters on fractions of it from one sixteenth to the whole. At every fraction evaluate on a held-out benchmark with annotator cue lists, using a keyword lexicon so no external judge is involved. Fit a curve of unsupported-cue rate against data amount to estimate where returns flatten, and compare with the same fractions of unverified captions.
CONTROLS: Compare each fraction against unverified captions of equal count and against the untuned model. Keep the learning rate, update schedule and clip set fixed, and repeat each fraction with three seeds.
COST: 780
PREDICTION: Verified data should lower unsupported-cue rate faster per example than unverified data, with returns flattening before the full set. The claim fails if the two curves overlap within seed spread.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cue-level probing benchmark for emotion hallucination in audiovisual models
PROPOSAL: Build a probing benchmark from clips in MAFW and DFEW, annotated by trained raters with the audio cues and visual cues that truly occur. Each clip receives multiple-choice questions on three kinds of cue: present and explanatory, present but irrelevant, and absent but typical of the labelled emotion. Score open-weight audiovisual language models by exact option choice, which removes any external judge and lets anyone replay the evaluation. Evaluate Qwen Omni, video-SALMONN and one tuned emotion captioner on the full clip set.
CONTROLS: Contrast each model against a text-only run that sees the question but not the clip, to measure what text priors alone answer. Compare against the same questions asked with the audio track removed and with the frames removed. Repeat scoring over several seeds and shuffled option orders. Report agreement with a second rater on a sampled subset.
COST: 96
PREDICTION: Text-only accuracy on absent-cue questions should sit clearly above chance, showing that language priors drive invented cues. The proposal fails if text-only accuracy stays near chance or if rater agreement on the cue lists is low.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Option-format scoring suite for emotion questions in audiovisual models
PROPOSAL: Assemble a question suite from clips in MELD and CREMA-D, with written answer keys drafted from the emotion labels shipped with each corpus. Each clip receives multiple-choice questions on three kinds of content: the labelled emotion, the gender of the speaker, and the scene type. Score open-weight audiovisual language models by exact option choice, without any external judge, and anyone can replay it. Evaluate Qwen Omni, video-SALMONN and one tuned emotion captioner on the full clip set.
CONTROLS: Compare each model against a uniform-guess run that picks options blindly, to measure what chance-level answers score. Compare against the same questions asked with the option list shortened and with the option list lengthened. Repeat scoring over several seeds and shuffled option orders. Report agreement with a second rater on a sampled subset.
COST: 96
PREDICTION: Gender and scene accuracy should sit clearly above chance, showing that the suite separates strong models from weak ones. The proposal fails if every model stays near chance or if rater agreement on the answer keys is low.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cue-contrastive preference tuning for grounded emotion explanations
PROPOSAL: Construct preference pairs from emotion clips: the preferred explanation cites cues verified in the audio and frames, the rejected one swaps in a plausible but absent cue or an irrelevant present cue. Fine-tune an audiovisual language model with Direct Preference Optimization using low-rank adapters on the language backbone. Produce the rejected explanations by prompting the model with the clip masked, so its own text priors write the invented cues. Evaluate on a held-out cue benchmark and on emotion keyword accuracy.
CONTROLS: Contrast with supervised fine-tuning on the preferred explanations alone, using the same clips and the same adapter rank. Compare against preference pairs whose rejected explanation comes from a different clip rather than from the masked run. Hold the clip set, the learning rate and the update count fixed across runs. Repeat training over several seeds and report the spread.
COST: 310
PREDICTION: Unsupported cues in held-out explanations should fall relative to the supervised run, with keyword accuracy kept. The method fails if the cross-clip rejected pairs reach the same reduction, because the masked-run negatives then contribute little.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adapter-rank study for preference tuning of emotion captions
PROPOSAL: Construct preference pairs from emotion clips: the preferred caption is the gold text written by annotators, the rejected one is a caption sampled from the untuned model at a higher temperature. Fine-tune an audiovisual language model with Direct Preference Optimization using low-rank adapters on the language backbone. Choose the adapter rank and the preference strength from a short list on a validation split. Evaluate on a held-out cue benchmark and on emotion keyword accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare against supervised fine-tuning on the preferred captions alone, run at several adapter ranks and preference strengths. Compare against a run whose rejected captions come from a different decoding temperature rather than from the default. Hold the clip set, the data order and the learning rate fixed across runs. Repeat training over several seeds and report the spread.
COST: 310
PREDICTION: Held-out caption quality should improve over the untuned model, with keyword accuracy kept. The study fails if every rank and strength reaches the same scores, because the tuned choices then contribute little.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Frame-level grounding reward for audiovisual emotion explanations
PROPOSAL: Train an audiovisual language model with a group-based reinforcement learning rule on DFEW and MAFW clips, giving each sampled explanation a reward for cited cues that a facial action detector and a speech emotion model confirm in the clip, with a deduction for cues neither confirms. The policy must cite cues in multiple clause form so each can be checked. Test on clips with conflicting modalities, where face and voice carry different emotions and only one explains the label. Count how often the explanation names the modality that carries the labelled emotion.
CONTROLS: Compare on conflicting-modality clips against the same model trained with a reward on emotion keyword correctness only. Compare against clips where face and voice agree, held fixed in difficulty and length. Vary the weight of the cue term across several values. Repeat each run over several seeds and report the spread.
COST: 540
PREDICTION: Cue-checked reward training should raise the rate of naming the modality that carries the label on conflicting clips. It fails if agreeing clips show the same gain, because the effect then reflects easier clips rather than grounding.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Group-based reward tuning for emotion explanations on single-speaker scripts
PROPOSAL: Tune an audiovisual language model with a group-based reinforcement learning rule on studio recordings of actors reading fixed scripts in CREMA-D, granting each sampled explanation a reward for cited cues that a facial action detector and a speech emotion model confirm in the clip, with a deduction for cues neither confirms. The policy must cite cues in multiple clause form so each can be checked. Test on held-out actors reading those scripts, where lighting, background and sound stay constant. Count how often the explanation names the labelled emotion.
CONTROLS: Contrast on held-out actors with the same model trained using a reward on emotion keyword correctness only. Contrast with studio clips whose lighting and background stay constant, held fixed in difficulty and length. Vary the weight of the cue term across several values. Repeat each run over several seeds and report the spread.
COST: 540
PREDICTION: Cue-checked reward training should raise the rate of naming the labelled emotion on held-out actors. It fails if the keyword-only reward reaches the same rate, because the effect then reflects easy scripted speech rather than grounding.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Judge-free hallucination score for emotion explanations: metric validation
PROPOSAL: Define a replayable score: parse each explanation into cue phrases with a fixed lexicon, then check every phrase against annotator cue lists for the clip. The score is the share of cited cues that are present, and a second score is the share that explain the labelled emotion. Validate it on MAFW and DFEW explanations from four open audiovisual models. Correlate the lexicon score with human ratings of faithfulness collected on a sample of explanations, and with the judgement of an external language model on the same sample.
CONTROLS: Compare the lexicon score against human faithfulness ratings, using the same explanations and the same rating form. Compare against explanations whose cue phrases are shuffled across clips, so the score should collapse. Hold the parser and the cue lists fixed, and change the paraphrase style of the explanations. Redo the rating on a second batch of clips.
COST: 175
PREDICTION: The lexicon score should track human faithfulness ratings and collapse on shuffled explanations. The metric fails if its correlation with humans does not rise above that of explanation length.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Judge-free fluency score for emotion explanations: metric validation
PROPOSAL: Define a replayable score: parse each explanation into sentences with a fixed tokenizer, then compute the length-normalised log-likelihood of each sentence under a scoring language model. The score is the mean over sentences, and a second score is the share of sentences containing an emotion keyword. Validate it on MAFW and DFEW explanations from four open audiovisual models. Correlate the fluency score with human ratings of readability collected on a sample of explanations, and with the judgement of an external language model on the same sample.
CONTROLS: Compare the fluency score against human readability ratings, drawn from the explanations and the rating form used earlier. Compare against explanations whose sentences are reordered within a clip, so the score should dip slightly. Keep the tokenizer and the scoring model constant, and change the length of the explanations. Redo the rating on a second batch of clips.
COST: 175
PREDICTION: The fluency score should track human readability ratings and fall slightly on shuffled sentences. The metric fails if its correlation with humans does not rise above that of explanation length.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Does text-prior pressure explain invented cues? A modality-removal protocol
PROPOSAL: Test whether invented cues come from the language backbone by comparing explanations written with and without the clip. For each emotion in MAFW, select the cues that co-occur most often in annotator lists, such as tears and crying sounds. Prompt an open audiovisual model for an explanation given clips of that emotion that lack the cue, and count how often the model cites it anyway. Repeat with a text-only version of the same model. If the invented cue rate is similar with and without the clip, text priors explain it.
CONTROLS: Compare cue-citing rates on clips that lack the typical cue against clips that contain it, with the prompt held fixed. Compare with the text-only run of the same backbone, equated on emotion label and prompt wording. Vary the emotion category across the full label set. Repeat decoding over several seeds and report the spread.
COST: 62
PREDICTION: Cue-citing on clips that lack the typical cue should approach the text-only rate. The idea fails if the text-only rate is far lower, since the backbone is then not the source.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Does emotion difficulty explain invented cues? A label-frequency protocol
PROPOSAL: Check whether invented cues come from rare labels by contrasting explanations written for frequent classes and for rare classes. For each emotion in MAFW, select the clips whose annotator lists are longest, such as tears and crying sounds. Ask an open audiovisual model for an explanation of clips of that emotion that carry many cues, and tally how frequently the model cites any cue. Redo this with a smaller version of the same model. When the cue rate is similar for frequent and rare labels, class frequency explains it.
CONTROLS: Compare cue-citing rates on clips with long annotator lists and clips with short ones, with the prompt held fixed. Compare with the smaller run of the same family, equated on emotion label and prompt wording. Vary the emotion category across the full label set. Repeat decoding over several seeds and report the spread.
COST: 62
PREDICTION: Cue-citing on rare labels should approach the frequent-label rate. The idea fails if the rare-label rate is far lower, since class frequency is then not the source.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Counterfactual clip edits to test which cues drive emotion answers
PROPOSAL: Edit MAFW and DFEW clips so that exactly one cue changes at a time: mute the soundtrack, blur the face, recolour clothing, or add street noise. Ask open audiovisual language models for the emotion and the supporting reason before and after each edit. A model that grounds its answers should change them when an explanatory cue is edited and keep them when an irrelevant cue is edited. Score the pattern of changes with a fixed lexicon, so the evaluation needs no external judge and can be replayed on every checkpoint.
CONTROLS: Edits are applied to three hundred clips per emotion. Each edit type is run with several seeds, and the answers on unedited clips serve as the reference.
COST: 140
PREDICTION: Answers should move when explanatory cues change and stay when irrelevant ones change, for the better-grounded models. The test fails to separate models if all of them change answers at the same rate for both edit kinds.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Larger emotion label sets to test recognition coverage of audiovisual models
PROPOSAL: Extend MAFW and DFEW clips with a finer vocabulary of emotion keywords so that more states than the basic labels can be named. Ask open audiovisual language models for the emotion keywords before and after merging near-synonyms. A model that covers a wide range should name more distinct keywords and match annotator keywords closely. Score the keyword overlap with a fixed lexicon, so the evaluation needs no external judge and can be replayed on every checkpoint.
CONTROLS: Keywords are collected for three hundred clips per emotion. Each vocabulary variant is run with several seeds, and the answers with the basic labels serve as the reference.
COST: 140
PREDICTION: Answers should cover more distinct keywords and overlap annotators more for the better models. The test fails to separate models if all of them reach the same overlap for both vocabulary variants.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Contrasting decoding with the clip against decoding with the clip removed
PROPOSAL: Reduce invented cues by comparing, at every token, the output distribution given the full clip with the distribution given a blank frame and silence, and penalising tokens that stay likely when the clip is gone. Apply the rule to an open audiovisual language model on DFEW and MAFW clips, set the penalty strength on a validation split, and score explanations against annotator cue lists. The rule needs no new training data, and it targets directly the language-prior bias that adds typical cues.
CONTROLS: Runs use greedy decoding and nucleus sampling on the same clips, with the penalty strength varied across a short list. The rule is also applied with only the audio dropped and only the frames dropped.
COST: 520
PREDICTION: Invented cues should fall while emotion keyword accuracy stays close to greedy decoding. The direction fails if invented cues stay at the greedy rate for every penalty strength tried.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Lowering decoding temperature and widening beam search for emotion explanations
PROPOSAL: Reduce errors by changing, at every step, the sampling distribution through a lower temperature and a wider beam, and keeping the beams whose sequence score stays highest. Apply the rule to an open audiovisual language model on DFEW and MAFW clips, set the beam width on a validation split, and score explanations against annotator keyword lists. The rule needs no new training data, and it targets directly the repetition and the length drift that add filler phrases.
CONTROLS: Runs use greedy decoding and nucleus sampling on the same clips, with the beam width varied across a short list. The rule is also applied with only the temperature lowered and only the beam widened.
COST: 520
PREDICTION: Repeated phrases should fall while emotion keyword accuracy stays close to greedy decoding. The direction fails if repeated phrases stay at the greedy rate for every beam width tried.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Present-versus-absent cue questions as a replayable hallucination test
PROPOSAL: Ask yes or no questions about whether a stated audio or visual cue occurs in a clip, pairing each present cue with a matched absent cue that is typical of the same emotion, such as tears with crying sounds. Use MAFW and DFEW clips with annotator cue lists to write the questions. An audiovisual language model that invents cues will answer yes to the absent typical ones. Score accuracy on the matched pairs, with answers parsed by a fixed rule, so the test needs no external judge.
CONTROLS: Questions are balanced between present and absent cues, with the order of the pairs varied. The test is repeated with several seeds and with the clip removed.
COST: 75
PREDICTION: Models should answer yes to absent typical cues more often than to absent odd cues. The test fails to expose invented cues if accuracy on matched pairs is the same with the clip removed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Open caption overlap scores as a replayable test of emotion captions
PROPOSAL: Ask for free-form captions describing the emotional scene, pairing each model caption with a reference caption written by annotators for the same clip, such as a person weeping beside a window. Use MAFW and DFEW clips with annotator captions to build the references. An audiovisual language model with good coverage will produce captions that overlap the references. Score n-gram overlap and embedding similarity, with captions parsed by a fixed rule, so the test needs no external judge.
CONTROLS: References are balanced between short and long captions, with the order of the clips varied. The test is repeated with several seeds and with the clip removed.
COST: 75
PREDICTION: Models should reach higher overlap on clips of typical scenes than on clips of odd scenes. The test fails to separate models if overlap is the same with the clip removed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Verified cue captions for fine-tuning an audiovisual language model
PROPOSAL: Build instruction data in which every cue named in a caption has been confirmed by a specialised detector on the clip: a facial action model for expressions, a speech emotion model for prosody, and an audio event tagger for ambient sound. Draft captions with a pretrained audiovisual model, delete cue phrases that no detector confirms, and fine-tune an open model with low-rank adapters on the cleaned captions of MAFW and DFEW clips. Evaluate invented cues and irrelevant reasons on a held-out clip set.
CONTROLS: Runs fine-tune on the cleaned captions and on the uncleaned drafts with the same clips. Updates, learning rate and adapter rank are matched, and each run is repeated with several seeds.
COST: 880
PREDICTION: Cleaned captions should reduce invented cues and irrelevant reasons compared with drafts. The direction fails if the two runs show the same rates within the spread across seeds.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Class-balanced captions for fine-tuning an audiovisual language model
PROPOSAL: Build instruction data in which every emotion class appears equally often in the captions: a rebalanced sampler for rare classes, a loss weighting for rare labels, and an augmentation step for scarce clips. Draft captions with a pretrained audiovisual model, resample clips until the classes are even, and fine-tune an open model with low-rank adapters on the rebalanced captions of MAFW and DFEW clips. Evaluate macro recall and per-class accuracy on a held-out clip set.
CONTROLS: Runs fine-tune on the rebalanced captions and on the original drafts with the same clips. Updates, learning rate and adapter rank are matched, and each run is repeated with several seeds.
COST: 880
PREDICTION: Rebalanced captions should raise macro recall and per-class accuracy compared with drafts. The direction fails if the two runs show the same scores within the spread across seeds.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training-free attention steering toward clip tokens in emotion explanations
PROPOSAL: Locate attention heads in an open audiovisual language model whose weight on clip tokens is low when cue words are generated, using DFEW clips. Scale those heads down and boost the heads with high clip weight, then measure how often explanations cite cues missing from annotator lists and how often irrelevant but present cues, such as clothing colour, serve as the reason. The method touches only inference, so every checkpoint can be tested the same day.
CONTROLS: Interventions are applied to a chosen head set found on one half of the clips and tested on the other half. Head sets of the same size are scaled as references, and answers are repeated with several seeds.
COST: 230
PREDICTION: Boosting clip-attending heads should cut invented cues and irrelevant reasons more than scaling arbitrary heads. The direction fails if head sets chosen on one half do not transfer to the other half.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training-free layer pruning for faster emotion explanations in audiovisual models
PROPOSAL: Locate transformer layers in an open audiovisual language model whose output change is low when cue words are generated, using DFEW clips. Skip those layers and keep the layers with high output change, then measure how often explanations finish within a time limit and how often shortened outputs, such as one-word replies, serve as the answer. The method touches only inference, so every checkpoint can be tested the same day.
CONTROLS: Interventions use a chosen layer set found on one half of the clips and are tested on the other half. Layer sets of equal count are skipped as comparisons, and answers are collected again with several seeds.
COST: 230
PREDICTION: Skipping low-change layers should cut response time and keep keyword accuracy better than skipping arbitrary layers. The direction fails if layer sets chosen on one half do not transfer to the other half.
